title: Galen: ventricles, nerves, and animal spirits
text:
CHAPTER 1. EARLIEST IDEAS ABOUT THE BRAIN
SECTION 1.3. GALEN: VENTRICLES, NERVES, AND ANIMAL SPIRITS

A physician who experimented

Galen of Pergamon (born around 129 CE, died around 200 to 216 CE; the date of his death is uncertain) was a Greek physician who worked in the Roman Empire. He trained in Pergamon, Smyrna, and Alexandria, served for a time as physician to the gladiators in Pergamon, and then moved to Rome, where he became physician to several emperors, including Marcus Aurelius. He wrote an enormous amount: his surviving works fill many volumes, and they shaped Western and Islamic medicine for more than a thousand years.

For neuroscience, Galen matters for three reasons. First, he settled the brain versus heart debate within medicine by using experiments, not only argument. Second, he produced detailed descriptions of the brain, cranial nerves, and spinal cord, mostly from animal dissection. Third, he developed a theory of how the brain works, based on spirits flowing through the ventricles and nerves, which dominated thinking until the seventeenth century. Galen is a good example of a scientist who was right about a great deal and wrong about a great deal, and whose authority later slowed the correction of his errors.

Galen's sources of evidence

Human dissection was not practiced in Galen's Rome. Galen dissected animals: pigs, oxen, dogs, goats, and especially Barbary macaques, which he considered closest to humans. He also learned from treating wounded gladiators, whose injuries sometimes exposed internal structures. Because he projected animal anatomy onto humans, some of his descriptions are wrong for humans. The most famous example is the rete mirabile ("wonderful net"), a network of blood vessels at the base of the brain found in oxen and some other hoofed animals but not in humans. Galen gave it an important role in preparing spirits. Its absence in humans was only clearly established in the Renaissance, as we will see with Vesalius.

The experiments with the recurrent laryngeal nerve

Galen's most famous neuroscience experiment involved the voice. In public demonstrations, he worked on a living pig, which was squealing as animals do when restrained. He exposed and tied off (ligated) the nerves that run alongside the trachea, which we now call the recurrent laryngeal nerves. When these nerves were tied, the pig continued to struggle but stopped squealing. When the ligatures were released, the voice could return.

This demonstration was a direct attack on the cardiocentric view. The Stoics and Aristotelians argued that the voice, which expresses thought, must come from the heart, the seat of thought. Galen showed that the voice depends on nerves that ultimately connect to the brain. The heart was still beating; the animal was alive and struggling; but without the nerve, there was no voice. If thought and speech came from the heart, why should tying a thin cord of nerve tissue in the neck stop the voice?

From an engineering point of view, this is a clean intervention experiment. Galen did not merely observe. He manipulated a single variable (conduction through a specific nerve), he kept other things constant (the animal alive, the heart beating, the muscles otherwise intact), and he showed that the effect is reversible. These are the ingredients of a good experiment that still appear in modern methods like optogenetics, where a specific set of neurons is switched off and on.

Spinal cord transections

Galen also studied the spinal cord. He cut the spinal cord of animals at different levels and observed the results. Cutting it high in the neck caused breathing to stop and death; cutting it lower produced paralysis and loss of sensation below the level of the cut, while the parts of the body above the cut were spared. He also observed that a cut across only one side of the cord produced effects on the same side of the body below the cut. These results showed that the spinal cord is a conduit linking the brain with the body, and that its organization is segmental: each level serves certain parts of the body.

This is the same reasoning a technician uses to trace a bus line through a machine. If you cut the line at point A and everything downstream fails, and cutting at point B makes only things below B fail, you can infer the topology of the wiring.

Cranial nerves

Galen described several pairs of cranial nerves, the nerves that leave the brain directly rather than via the spinal cord. His classification combined some nerves that we now separate, so his list had seven pairs rather than the twelve recognized in modern anatomy. (The modern twelve-pair system is usually traced to the eighteenth-century anatomist Samuel Thomas von Soemmerring.) Galen's descriptions of the optic nerves, the nerves controlling the eye muscles, the trigeminal nerve, and others nevertheless formed the foundation of cranial nerve anatomy for centuries.

Hard and soft nerves

Galen proposed that nerves come in two broad types. Soft nerves, which he thought arose from the front of the brain, were for sensation, because sensation requires receiving impressions, and soft material takes impressions easily. Hard nerves, which he thought arose from the back of the brain and the spinal cord, were for movement, because moving the body requires strength. This is a theory derived from material properties, a kind of reasoning an engineer might recognize: choose the material for the job. The specific assignment is not correct, but the idea that sensory and motor pathways are different was correct and important. It was finally put on firm experimental ground in the early nineteenth century with the Bell-Magendie law, which states that the dorsal roots of the spinal cord carry sensory fibers and the ventral roots carry motor fibers.

The pneuma theory and the ventricles

Galen built on the earlier Alexandrian idea of pneuma. In a simplified form, his scheme worked like this:

1. Air drawn in by breathing provides the raw material for pneuma.
2. In the liver, food is turned into blood, which carries "natural spirit" for nutrition and growth.
3. In the heart, blood is mixed with pneuma from the lungs to produce "vital spirit," which travels in the arteries and gives warmth and life.
4. Vital spirit reaches the base of the brain, where (in Galen's account) the rete mirabile refines it further into "psychic pneuma," also translated as "animal spirit" (from the Latin anima, soul, not from "animal" as a creature).
5. Psychic pneuma is stored in the ventricles of the brain and flows out through the nerves to produce sensation and movement.

Galen did not simply say that thought takes place in the ventricles; he was more cautious and focused on the brain substance as well. But his followers in late antiquity and the Middle Ages developed what is called the cell doctrine, or ventricular localization theory, in which different mental faculties were assigned to different ventricles. A common medieval scheme placed perception and "common sense" (the integration of the senses) in the front ventricles, reasoning and judgment in the middle ventricle, and memory in the rear ventricle. Writers such as Nemesius, Augustine, and later Avicenna and Albertus Magnus discussed versions of this scheme, though the details varied from author to author. Medieval and Renaissance drawings often show the head with three circles in a row representing the "cells."

It is worth pausing on how strange and how reasonable this is. The ventricles are real, visible, fluid-filled cavities. They are the most obvious structural feature you see when you cut a brain open, apart from the folded surface. If you believe the mind works by moving a subtle fluid, then the cavities are the obvious place to store and process that fluid. The theory is a natural extension of a hydraulic model of the nervous system. It is wrong because the computation actually happens in the tissue, not the cavities. The ventricles contain cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the brain and helps clear waste, but they do not think.

Galen on the brain and the mind

Galen's broad conclusions about the brain were largely sound. He held that the brain is the source of the nerves and the seat of the "ruling part" of the soul, responsible for sensation, voluntary movement, and thought. He recognized that brain injuries and pressure on the brain could affect consciousness; he reported that pressing on certain parts of the exposed brain in animals could make them lose sensation and movement, and that pressing on the ventricles in particular had dramatic effects. He tied many mental disturbances to disorders of the brain. On these points he was right, and his authority helped make the encephalocentric view standard in medicine.

Galen's legacy

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, Galen's works were preserved and studied in the Byzantine world and translated into Syriac and Arabic. Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a ninth-century translator in Baghdad, translated a large number of Galen's works and is a key figure in this transmission. Physicians of the Islamic world, including al-Razi (Rhazes) and Ibn Sina (Avicenna), built on Galen and added their own observations. From the eleventh and twelfth centuries onward, Arabic versions and Greek originals were translated into Latin and entered the medical curricula of European universities.

Over time, Galen became an authority whose statements were taught as established fact. In many medieval and early Renaissance universities, anatomy lessons involved a lecturer reading from a Galenic text while an assistant pointed to structures on a body. When the body did not match the text, the body was sometimes thought to be at fault. This is the background against which Vesalius made his break in the sixteenth century.

The lesson here is not that Galen was a bad scientist. By the standards of his time, he was an outstanding experimenter. The lesson is about how knowledge is maintained. A body of knowledge that is not continually checked against new data tends to fossilize, errors and all.

Bridge to AI: hydraulic models, information flow, and the danger of authority

Galen's pneuma theory is a theory of information flow, even though it uses fluid. Spirits are produced, refined, stored, and distributed. In modern neuroscience, we replace the spirit with electrical and chemical signals, but we still talk about "flow" of information through pathways, about "processing stages," and about "storage." Neural network diagrams that show data flowing from input layer to output layer are, in a sense, very distant descendants of the diagrams of the three ventricular cells, with perception at the front, reasoning in the middle, and memory at the back. Many simple AI architectures have exactly this form: an encoder that turns input into a representation, a processing module, and a memory module.

But the brain does not separate these neatly, and neither do the most capable modern AI systems. In a transformer language model, for example, knowledge storage, pattern recognition, and something like reasoning are mixed in the same layers of weights. Interpretability researchers have found evidence that some kinds of factual association are concentrated in particular layers, which is a bit like a cell doctrine for networks, but the picture is far from a clean three-box diagram.

The other lesson is about the danger of authority. In machine learning, benchmark results and influential papers can play the role that Galen played: a reference point that people trust without rechecking. Good engineering practice, like Vesalius's anatomy, requires going back to the data, rerunning the experiment, and being willing to say that the textbook is wrong.

Summary

- Galen, a second-century physician in the Roman Empire, used animal dissection and experiment to argue that the brain, not the heart, controls sensation, movement, and voice.
- His ligation of the recurrent laryngeal nerve in a living pig silenced the animal's squeal, a clear intervention experiment.
- His spinal cord transections revealed the cord's role as a conduit and its segmental organization.
- He described cranial nerves and proposed that sensory and motor nerves differ.
- His theory of pneuma and animal spirits, together with the later medieval "cell doctrine," placed mental functions in the ventricles. This was wrong but natural under a hydraulic model.
- His works dominated medicine for more than a thousand years, which delayed correction of errors that arose from relying on animal anatomy.
